title: I said I’d come back after a year. I released the EA in March, so here’s the honest progress update instead.
author: Loose-Object-8913
selftext:
A while back I posted about a Gold EA I was building, and someone pointed out that it hadn’t been live long enough to judge properly.

Fair point.

I jokingly said I’d come back in March, but the funny part is I only actually released the EA this March, so I’m still not here claiming a full-year miracle robot.

Instead, this is just an honest progress update.

Since release, I’ve been working on OmegaGold Pro, a rule-based XAUUSD EA for MT5. The current V2 build uses an M1 scalper system with fixed timed exits, broker-side SL protection, and diagnostic tracking for live position management.

The biggest lesson so far has been that backtests are only one part of the story. Broker conditions, VPS behaviour, execution, spreads, and live state management can all expose things you don’t see immediately in tester.

Recently I had a client case where the entries matched tester results almost perfectly, but a couple of live trades stayed open longer than expected. That pushed me to build a diagnostic version that tracks exactly what the scalper is doing: trade state, close timing, position recovery, and whether close requests are actually being sent.

So no, I’m not here saying “this is proven for years.” It isn’t.

I’m here saying I’ve released it, maintained it, updated it, and I’m trying to build it in public honestly instead of pretending it never has rough weeks.

If anyone here builds or runs EAs, I’d be interested to hear how you deal with live-vs-tester differences, especially around broker execution and position state recovery.

And yes, I know. I said March. I got there eventually, just not in the way I meant.

replies.author: Loose-Object-8913
replies.body:
No, the source code isn’t public. It’s a commercial MQL5 product, so only the compiled EA is available through the Market.  
Happy to discuss the logic at a high level though: it’s a rule-based XAUUSD EA with M1 scalper execution, timed position management, broker-side SL protection, and no martingale/grid.

comments.author: Tight_Papaya_2164
comments.body: What is your edge and how did you find it?

replies.author: Loose-Object-8913
replies.body: Mostly trend + pullback/continuation setups with strict risk and execution rules. I found it by testing loads of ideas, killing the ones that fell apart, and keeping what still held up across different years, delays and live trading 😂

replies.author: Tight_Papaya_2164
replies.body:
If "held up in live trading" was part of how you decided which version to keep, then live wasn't a test of the strategy, it was part of picking it. The same data can't both choose the winner and prove the winner works. For a clean read you'd have to lock the settings, write down the date, and only count what happens after that.

Other thing is how many genuinely different ideas you went through. If you try 10 unrelated ones and keep the best, that best one shows a t-stat around 1.5 even when all 10 are pure noise. At 100 it's about 2.5. Worth saying that only counts distinct ideas, not parameter tweaks of the same one, since those all move together and don't add much.

And the thing that actually decides how long you need is the Sharpe, not the trade count. t is roughly Sharpe times the square root of years. So at Sharpe 1.5 you'd know in about a year, at 1.0 it's closer to three, at 0.5 it's a decade. Trading more often gets you a cleaner read on the per-trade edge but doesn't speed up the calendar.

So roughly how many genuinely different ideas did you test? And was live used to pick between them, or just to check one you'd already locked?

replies.author: Loose-Object-8913
replies.body:
Yeah that’s a fair challenge. I’d separate “ideas” from “versions” though, I’ve probably tested a handful of genuinely different setup families, then a lot of variations inside them. Most got killed pretty quickly.  
And no, I don’t use live results to keep changing the strategy until it looks good. Once I’m happy with a version I lock it, then live is mainly checking whether the thing behaves the same outside the tester fills, timing, spread, broker differences, trade management etc.  
So I’d say backtests are where I select the idea, forward/live is where I find out if the implementation is actually real.

replies.author: Tight_Papaya_2164
replies.body:
One thing still worth chewing on. If backtests pick the idea and live only checks the implementation, the idea itself never gets tested out of sample. Live proving the fills and spread match the tester tells you the code is honest. It doesn't tell you the thing it's honestly running makes money. Two different questions, and the second one is still leaning on the backtest.

Since you asked about live vs tester, here's ours. We ran an opening range breakout on SPY and QQQ over 10 years of 1-minute data. Sharpe by cost per side came out 0.30 at zero, 0.14 at a penny, −0.01 at two cents, −0.17 at three. Died between one and two cents. The published versions of that strategy quoting +1,484% turned out to be the zero-cost column with leverage on top.

Different setup to yours and equities not gold, so I'm not saying it transfers. But the shape of it is what I'd watch for.

Two things that caught us out. 2020 was the worst year of the lot for both, so the high-vol regime everyone treats as the sweet spot was actually the bad one. And our minute data puller had a daylight savings bug in the session window that quietly dropped about 35% of winter volume, including the close. Backtest looked fine, data was wrong. Gold runs nearly 24 hours with a daily break, so that's exactly where I'd go looking.

What does your live vs tester slippage actually look like? Average spread you actually paid versus what the tester assumed. That's the number that settled it for us, and you're probably the only one here who has it for gold on M1.

replies.author: Loose-Object-8913
replies.body:
Haha yeah, now you’re getting into the part I’m actually working on 😂 I agree execution matching doesn’t prove the edge itself. My live comparison so far has mainly been about whether the EA is doing what the tester says it should.  
I haven’t got a clean enough live sample yet to claim that as independent proof of profitability. What I *do* have is the same trades appearing extremely close across different brokers, and that’s what got me digging into spread/slippage and broker-time differences next. I’m actually going to quantify average live spread/slippage vs tester because you’re right, that’s a much better number than just saying “the trades look similar.”

replies.author: Tight_Papaya_2164
replies.body:
If the trades come out nearly identical across brokers, those are basically the same series. So it's one sample seen three times, not three samples. Doesn't really tell you whether it makes money.

The differences do though. Same trades, different spreads, different fills, so the gap in net P&L between your brokers is a straight measurement of how much execution is costing you. That's the slippage number you said you're about to go measure. You already have it, it's just sitting on the wrong axis.

Other thing a clean enough sample is something you can work out rather than wait for. t is roughly Sharpe times root years. We measured seven published retail systems recently and their backtested Sharpes of 0.87 to 1.09 came out between 0.17 and 0.56 live, median around 0.42. So live ran at about 43% of backtest. Those were monthly systems not scalpers, so treat it as a rough prior rather than gospel.

Apply it though and it gets concrete. Backtest Sharpe of 2 means expect roughly 0.86 live, which is about 3.7 years to prove. Backtest 1.5 is 6.5 years. Backtest 1.0 is fourteen. Worth knowing which one you're signing up for before you commit to the wait.

And you don't need significance to learn something. Six months in you can already work out implied live Sharpe, t divided by root years, and compare it against backtest times 0.43. If it's tracking, fine. If it's a fifth of it, you know now instead of in year four.

What's your backtest Sharpe out of interest? With that plus your cross-broker spread you could pin the timeline down pretty tightly.

(This kind of thing is what I do as paid work, but you're close enough to the answer on your own that I'd just measure the broker gap first and see what it tells you.)

replies.author: Loose-Object-8913
replies.body:
Yeah I get what you mean now 😂 Same trades across brokers isn’t extra proof, but the P&L difference between them is basically showing me what execution is costing.  
I don’t want to just invent a Sharpe number either haha. I need to pull it properly from the exact version I’ve got locked now.  
So yeah, I’m gonna look at that broker gap first, then compare the live numbers properly instead of just saying “it looks close” 😂
